rv.q: Directed by Phyllida Lloyd, this production out of London reminds us that casting against the grain can be a potent tool in theater.
And yet by overdoing the concept, the production undermines it.
Unfortunately, the prison setting, while certainly novel, adds little to our appreciation of the play.
All this fudging seems to point to a problem with the framing structure and the way it may impede rather than excite the storytelling.
This videoed performance is a stunning example of that.
Sophie Stanton's Falstaff is a sly treat, the best portrayal of the part I've seen.
Nonetheless, strong performances and clever touches abound, making it a worthy if not revelatory experience.
Nevertheless, after a while, you just go along with the concept, which brings a rough vigor and punk aesthetic to the familiar drama.
Unfortunately, Lloyd's women's-prison setting is not nearly as illuminating here as it was in was with Caesar.
As a result, this Henry IV is both tantalizing and something of a missed opportunity.
Director Phyllida Lloyd used a similar framing for 2013's Julius Caesar also at St. Ann's, but it is less successful here.

cn.t: Lloyd's all-female, prison-set Henry IV divides critics: some praise its sharp wit and entertaining performances, while others find the concept less effective than her previous Julius Caesar, with a disappointingly restrained Falstaff.
